# Directives and crawl budget

Disallowed URLs are not fetched, so they cost no crawl budget. Pages with noindex must be fetched, so they do; nofollow is a hint, not a block, so the linked URLs can still be crawled, and crawl-delay is ignored by Googlebot. Day 2 stressed that robots.txt does not control indexing: a disallowed URL can still appear in results without its content, and a noindex on a blocked URL is never seen. John Mueller advised against the page-level nofollow robots rule, which stops signals passing through every link on the page, in favour of rel=nofollow on individual links. He also said AI crawlers do not really know what to do with nofollow, without saying whose crawlers he meant (not in Google's docs). A second recording of Day 1 explained the slide on nofollow: Google does not crawl through the nofollow link itself but still crawls the linked page when it finds it through other links, as Google's 2017 crawl budget post also says. A second recording of Day 2 confirmed John Mueller's remark that if robots meta tags were reinvented today the page-level nofollow rule would probably not be part of them. Day 2's opening Q&A illustrated why a disallow is not a noindex with a national tax authority that blocks very important PDFs, whose URLs Google can show without their content, and John Mueller said robots meta rules only work if robots.txt allows the fetch. Disallowing an image or video file keeps it out of Google, and a disallowed video is not shown by its bare URL. In the Day 1 Q&A Gary Illyes said disallowing a section such as /ads shifts crawl budget to the rest of the site. Author's view: Google's guide says freed crawl budget shifts only on sites already at their capacity limit, so block only sections you never want crawled.

Based on: `D1-C105`, `D1-C106`, `D1-C107`, `D1-C127`, `D1-C108`, `D2-C058`, `D2-C021`, `D2-C022`, `D2-C069`, `D2-C063`, `D2-C064`, `D2-C066`, `D1-C109`, `D1-C071`, `D2-C065`, `D2-C067`, `D2-C529`, `D2-C530`, `D2-C821`, `D2-C844`, `D2-C846`, `D2-C850`, `D2-C851`, `D2-C932`, `D2-C933`, `D1-C469`, `D1-C470`, `D2-C849`.

## What to do

- Use noindex to keep pages out of the index, not to save crawling.
- Never disallow a URL whose noindex you need Google to see.
- Replace a page-level nofollow robots rule with rel=nofollow on the specific links that need it.
- To slow Google temporarily, return 503 or 429.
- To keep AI crawlers away from content, use robots.txt rules for those crawlers, not nofollow.
- To keep images out of Google, use a robots.txt disallow (for example for Googlebot-Image) or a noindex X-Robots-Tag header.

## What Google's documentation says

- **[Docs]** Google supports only the user-agent, allow, disallow and sitemap fields in robots.txt. Other fields such as crawl-delay are not supported.
  <br><sub>`D1-C084` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google interprets robots.txt · is the documentation · [How Google interprets the robots.txt specification](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec) · Extended by [D1-C516](../../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) · Extended by [D2-C017](../../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extended by [D2-C842](../../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Used by `DEV-SRV-05`, the glossary term *robots.txt*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google treats nofollow as a hint for crawling, not a block: nofollow links will generally not be followed, but the linked pages may still be crawled if Google finds them through sitemaps or other links. To stop Google fetching URLs on your own site, use a robots.txt disallow rule.
  <br><sub>`D1-C127` · Google Search Central, Search Central blog (10 September 2019) · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · is the documentation · [Qualify your outbound links to Google](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/qualify-outbound-links), [Evolving "nofollow" – new ways to identify the nature of links](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2019/09/evolving-nofollow-new-ways-to-identify) · Extended by [D2-C067](../../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-02`, `DEV-IDX-06`, the glossary term *nofollow*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google advises against using noindex to save crawl budget and against using robots.txt to temporarily reallocate budget. Use robots.txt only for pages you never want crawled, and 404 or 410 for removed pages.
  <br><sub>`D1-C109` · Google · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · is the documentation · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Used by `DEV-ERR-01`, `DEV-IDX-02`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's noindex documentation says the noindex rule works only if the page is not blocked by robots.txt: a crawler that cannot fetch the page never sees the rule, and the page can still appear in search results, for example if other pages link to it.
  <br><sub>`D2-C022` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · is the documentation · [Block Search indexing with noindex](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/block-indexing) · Extends [D1-C106](../../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`, the glossary term *noindex*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's documented ways to keep a site's images out of search results are a robots.txt disallow rule (for example for Googlebot-Image) or a noindex X-Robots-Tag HTTP header, with the Removals tool for emergencies.
  <br><sub>`D2-C529` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos · is the documentation · [Remove images hosted on your site from search results](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/prevent-images-on-your-page) · Used by `DEV-IDX-03`, `DEV-IMG-06`, the glossary term *X-Robots-Tag*</sub>

## Analysis

- **[Analysis]** A URL blocked in robots.txt can still be indexed without its content if other pages link to it, and Google cannot see a noindex on a page it is not allowed to fetch.
  <br><sub>`D1-C110` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, How Google thinks about crawl budget · Extended by [D2-C020](../../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extended by [D2-C846](../../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extended by [D2-C849](../../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) · Extended by [D2-C058](../../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Repeated by [D2-C850](../../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Repeated by [D2-C851](../../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Google's crawl budget guide says crawl budget freed by robots.txt blocks is not shifted to other pages unless the site already hits its crawl capacity limit, and advises against robots.txt for temporary reallocation; so block only sections you never want crawled, and expect a shift only on capacity-limited sites.
  <br><sub>`D1-C470` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 1, Q&A · [Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget) · Extends [D1-C469](../../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Explain robots.txt and noindex to developers as two separate controls: robots.txt controls crawling, noindex controls indexing. To keep a page out of Search, let Google crawl it and serve noindex; a robots.txt disallow alone can leave the bare URL in results.
  <br><sub>`D2-C023` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · Used by `DEV-IDX-01`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Google's robots.txt introduction names links from elsewhere on the web as the reason a disallowed URL can still be indexed, while on stage Google spoke of the URL's importance; either way, well-linked important URLs are the disallowed ones most likely to appear in results, so keep such pages crawlable with noindex if they must stay out of Search.
  <br><sub>`D2-C849` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Welcome to indexing day! · Extends [D1-C110](../../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Audit robots meta tags set by templates and plug-ins: an explicit all rule does nothing and can go, while a page-level nofollow strips link signals from every link on the page and is better replaced by qualifying only the specific links that need it.
  <br><sub>`D2-C065` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing · Used by `DEV-IDX-06`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** nofollow is a link-graph hint for search engines, not an access control: to keep AI crawlers away from content, use robots.txt rules for the specific crawlers; at Google, Google-Extended covers Gemini training and grounding, and the Search generative AI control covers AI Overviews and AI Mode.
  <br><sub>`D2-C067` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Controlling indexing · Extends [D1-C127](../../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Extends [D1-C482](../../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Hiding an image as a CSS background is a fragile way to keep it out of Google: it only stops extraction from that page, so the same image URL used in an img element elsewhere or listed in a sitemap can still be indexed; the documented robots.txt or noindex X-Robots-Tag methods are the reliable route.
  <br><sub>`D2-C530` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Using images to your advantage and Engaging Search users with videos · [Remove images hosted on your site from search results](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/prevent-images-on-your-page), [Google image SEO best practices](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/google-images) · Used by `DEV-IMG-06`</sub>

## Built on these claims

The items of the developer and content kits that rest on this topic's claims.

- Requirement `DEV-ERR-01`: Return 404 or 410 for removed and non-existent URLs
- Requirement `DEV-IDX-01`: Use noindex to keep a page out of Search, and leave that URL crawlable
- Requirement `DEV-IDX-02`: Do not use noindex, nofollow or crawl-delay to save crawl budget
- Requirement `DEV-IDX-03`: Send robots rules for PDFs, images and other non-HTML files in the X-Robots-Tag header
- Requirement `DEV-IDX-06`: Prefer rel attributes on individual links to a page-level nofollow
- Requirement `DEV-IMG-06`: Keep images out of Search with robots.txt or X-Robots-Tag, not with CSS tricks
- Requirement `DEV-SRV-05`: Rely only on the fields Google supports (user-agent, allow, disallow, sitemap) and keep robots.txt under 500 KiB
- Requirement `DEV-URL-08`: Keep faceted navigation out of the crawl with robots.txt rules or URL fragments
- Requirement `DEV-VID-06`: Serve videos fast in a common container with standard codecs, and never block the files
- Fact `F-025`: noindex costs crawl budget because Google must fetch a page to see the rule, while URLs disallowed in robots.txt are not fetched at all.
- Glossary term *Googlebot-Image and Googlebot-Video*
- Glossary term *nofollow*
- Glossary term *noindex*
- Glossary term *robots.txt*
